I was noticing this same problem and tried to dig into what was causing the issue.
Ultimately each migration script was getting `require()`'d sequentially within TypeORM code. The require was taking about a half second per script, which makes sense if it was having to resolve and compile each from scratch.

I also noticed that in my tsconfig.json I wasn't including the migration directory. I ended up adding "migration/**/*.ts" to the include directive, and now it's loading fast. Hopefully that resolves what you're seeing as well.

I am having this problem too, and it's painful continue to work like this. Our project has 110+ migrations, using ts-node and the migration folder on tsconfig.json. The startup on the project is affected as well, mainly when starting the conections with `createConnection()`. I don't have a clue how to procede.

Can anyone consistently reproduce this issue?

I've managed to get a CPU profile of it happening, but then if I subsequently call `migration:run` again in a separate process it's fast. I suspect because some caching is going on either at the node / v8 level.

I'm having this issue too, we currently have ~70 migrations and it takes times to finish (up to 2-3 minutes on slow cpu).
I'v managed to fix this problem using the builded javascript (*.js), it now takes few seconds.

`createConnection` is faster with javascript files (< 100ms) vs typescript (~ 20 secs)
@pleerock Are there any updates to this?
Have the same problem with `createConnection()` taking about 50 seconds -- I have 42 migrations.  If I set `TYPEORM_MIGRATIONS=[]` it's essentially instant (less than a second).

We actually solved these problems by adding the `--transpile-only` ts-node flag to the npm script that runs the migrations. Reduced our run time ten-fold and is pretty safe as you don't really need to check your typescript syntax when you run migrations. Then we also squashed all of our migrations, which gave us even more performance improvements. All in all, these two changes got us from 120 second runs down to 4 seconds.

Unrelated to this issue, but when I try `--transpile-only` with ts-node, I get an error with the Postgres driver:

> Something what I don't understand is why `createConnection()` reads migration files - the method itself does not need them AFAIK. They are only needed by migration commands.
> 
> My current workaround is:
> 
> ```ts
> // ormconfig.ts
> 
> module.exports =  {
>   name: 'default',
>   type: 'postgres',
>   uuidExtension: 'pgcrypto',
>   synchronize: false,
>   migrations: process.env.SKIP_MIGRATIONS ? [] : ['src/migrations/*.js', 'src/migrations/*.ts'],
> }
> 
> // package.json
> 
> {
>   "scripts": {
>     "start": "SKIP_MIGRATIONS=1 yarn nodemon --exec node -r module-alias/register -r ts-node/register ./src/containers/api.ts", // used to start app locally for development
>   }
> }
> ```
> 
> Now `createConnection()` takes **5 sec** instead of **55 sec** (there are 74 migrations in the project) when starting app locally.
> Would be nice if only migration commands read migration files out of the box.

The migrations can be set to run when connecting:

> migrationsRun - Indicates if migrations should be auto run on every application launch. As an alternative, you can use CLI and run migration:run command.

issue.title: Choose a ORM for node-based services

repository.name: bloom
repository.description: Bloom is Exygy’s affordable housing platform. Bloom's goal is to be a single entry point for affordable housing seekers and a hub for application and listing management for developers.

issue.body:
Assuming we continue down the path of node-based reference implementations for the core services, the next major decision we'll need to make is an ORM for database operations. Postgres is the presumptive database, perhaps with an HA variant in the future, but not on the immediate horizon.

In addition to good postgres support, we also want enough Typescript support that we won't need to be casting every result set or otherwise writing too much boilerplate.

Options to consider include:

- [TypeORM](https://typeorm.io/)
- [Prisma2](https://www.prisma.io/)
- [Objection](https://github.com/Vincit/objection.js) / [Knex](http://knexjs.org/)
- [Sequelize](https://github.com/sequelize/sequelize)

I think we're open to other options, as well, so long as they meet our core needs and have a fighting chance at long-term sustainability.

There's also still the option of choosing something like [NestJS](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/database) as a more full featured backend framework, which would then likely imply (though not conclusively) using their TypeORM integration. It's still not clear we need all of those features, though.
